purpose: Source-backed retrieval, exam prompts, and the complete teacher-assigned DSA5104 homework set.

questions.prompt: Why does a DBMS need integrity constraints instead of leaving every rule in application code?
accepted: constraints are centralized
prevent invalid states
database enforces integrity
questions.solution: Constraints make validity rules explicit and enforceable across users and applications, rather than relying on every program to reproduce them correctly.
questions.explanation: The lecture connects explicit integrity with consistency, maintainability, and safer shared access.
questions.misconception: A database is not only a passive file store.
questions.visualHook: Point to the logical level and data dictionary.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct?
choices: An instance is the permanent design
A schema is the current rows only
A schema describes structure and an instance is current contents
A view is the same as a disk block
questions.explanation: Schema and instance are the design/current-state distinction used throughout the relational model.
questions.misconception: Do not treat a table definition and its current rows as the same object.
questions.visualHook: Use the schema-versus-instance lab.

questions.prompt: Given Department(id) and Student(id, department_id), state the key and foreign-key constraints for a one-to-many relationship.
accepted: Department.id primary key and Student.department_id foreign key references Department.id
student department_id references department id
questions.solution: Declare Department.id as the primary key and Student.department_id as a foreign key referencing Department.id. The foreign key is on the many side.
questions.explanation: The mapping preserves one department with many student tuples while enforcing referential integrity.
questions.misconception: The foreign key does not belong on the one-side relation for this simple mapping.
questions.visualHook: Follow the identity edge in the keys lab.

questions.prompt: Why is a generated numeric identifier not automatically a good business key?
accepted: unique is not stable meaning
identity lifecycle matters
it may not be stable across systems
questions.solution: Uniqueness is only one requirement. A business key also needs appropriate stability, integration behavior, and meaning for the system's lifecycle.
questions.explanation: Database identity and business identity can be different design decisions.
questions.misconception: Unique does not imply meaningful or stable.
questions.visualHook: Compare candidate-key choices before selecting a primary key.

questions.prompt: Translate a many-to-many Student–Club relationship into a relational schema.
accepted: membership relation with student_id and club_id
create relationship table with both foreign keys
composite key student_id club_id
questions.solution: Create Student and Club relations with their keys, then Membership(student_id, club_id, membership_attributes) with foreign keys to both and typically a composite primary key.
questions.explanation: A relationship relation preserves multiplicity and makes relationship attributes explicit.
questions.misconception: Do not store an unbounded repeating list inside one entity tuple.
questions.visualHook: Use the ER-to-relational design decision tree.

questions.prompt: Which choice belongs to physical design?
choices: Choose entity attributes
Choose relation schemas
Choose an index or storage layout
Define a business relationship
questions.explanation: Physical design chooses layout and access methods after logical meaning and constraints are established.
questions.misconception: Indexes are physical access methods, not a substitute for logical modeling.
questions.visualHook: Place the choice on the logical-to-physical design boundary.

questions.prompt: A joined table has department counts 2, 1, and 3. Which groups remain after HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2?
accepted: departments with counts 2 and 3
2 and 3
two groups
questions.solution: The groups with counts 2 and 3 remain; the group with count 1 is filtered after aggregation.
questions.explanation: HAVING evaluates the aggregate result for each completed group.
questions.misconception: The count does not exist at the row-filtering stage.
questions.visualHook: Advance the SQL semantics trace to the aggregate-filter step.

questions.prompt: Why can moving a predicate from HAVING to WHERE change the result?
accepted: where filters rows before grouping
having filters groups after aggregation
aggregate is not available in where
questions.solution: WHERE changes which rows enter each group, while HAVING removes completed groups. An aggregate predicate therefore belongs in HAVING.
questions.explanation: The distinction is semantic even if an optimizer later rewrites a safe row-local predicate.
questions.misconception: Textual clause order and logical evaluation meaning are related but not identical.
questions.visualHook: Compare the WHERE and HAVING nodes in the lab.

questions.prompt: What must stay unchanged when the optimizer replaces a full scan with an index lookup?
accepted: logical result
relation result
query semantics
questions.solution: The logical relation result must remain unchanged; only the physical access path changes.
questions.explanation: Optimization is allowed to change execution cost, not declarative meaning.
questions.misconception: A faster plan is not a different answer.
questions.visualHook: Follow the query processor pipeline from plan choice to result.

questions.prompt: Which component chooses a low-cost evaluation plan from alternatives?
choices: DML compiler/query optimizer
Data dictionary only
View level
Foreign key
questions.explanation: The DML compiler performs query optimization and the query evaluation engine executes the selected plan.
questions.misconception: The parser and evaluator have different jobs from the optimizer.
questions.visualHook: Select the optimize stage in the pipeline lab.

questions.prompt: Explain why a transfer of amount a should update A and B within one transaction.
accepted: avoid partial update
atomicity
all or nothing
questions.solution: The updates $A\leftarrow A-a$ and $B\leftarrow B+a$ implement one logical function. A single transaction prevents a crash between them from committing only one update.
questions.explanation: Transaction boundaries follow business invariants rather than statement count.
questions.misconception: Two individually valid writes can still violate a cross-row invariant when separated.
questions.visualHook: Use the transaction safety map.

questions.prompt: What work is shifted when a team chooses schema-on-read?
accepted: validation moves to query time
interpretation deferred
consumers validate later
questions.solution: Schema-on-read makes ingestion flexible but moves interpretation, validation, and sometimes error discovery toward query and consumer time.
questions.explanation: The representation choice changes when agreement is enforced; it does not eliminate the need for agreement.
questions.misconception: Flexible ingestion is not the same as no schema.
questions.visualHook: Adjust the flexibility explorer and inspect the validation trade-off.

questions.prompt: Given the foreign-key constraint from instructor.dept_name to the department relation, give an example insert that would violate the constraint.
accepted: insert a tuple whose dept_name is absent from department
insert (10111, Ostrom, Economics, 110000) when Economics is missing
questions.solution: Inserting (10111, Ostrom, Economics, 110000) into instructor when the department relation has no Economics tuple violates the foreign-key constraint, because dept_name must refer to an existing department.
questions.explanation: A foreign key is enforced: SQL rejects any insert whose referenced value does not exist in the referenced relation.
questions.misconception: A foreign key is not optional metadata; insertions are checked.
questions.visualHook: Trace the dept_name foreign-key edge in the keys lab.

questions.prompt: Using the employee database, write a relational-algebra expression (select, project, join) for the names of every employee who lives in city "Miami" and whose salary is greater than USD 100,000.
accepted: project person_name from select on city and salary over employee join works
expression with sigma, pi, and bowtie
questions.solution: Join employee with works, select rows whose city is Miami and whose salary exceeds USD 100,000, then project person_name. The join brings the salary attribute from works into employee so one selection can combine both predicates.
questions.explanation: The join combines employee and works so one selection can reference both city and salary before projection keeps only the name.
questions.misconception: Do not select on salary directly over employee before joining works, because salary does not live in employee.
questions.visualHook: Follow the join-before-select ordering in the algebra lab.

questions.prompt: In the bank database, assume branch names and customer names uniquely identify branches and customers. What primary keys do you choose, and which foreign keys follow?
accepted: branch_name primary key for branch; customer_name primary key for customer
foreign keys on account, loan, depositor, borrower referencing branch and customer
questions.solution: branch_name is the primary key of branch and customer_name the primary key of customer. The relationship relations (account, loan, depositor, and borrower) carry foreign keys referencing branch and/or customer as their connections require.
questions.explanation: Primary keys carry identity; foreign keys encode the references between relations and enforce referential integrity.
questions.misconception: A relationship table may be associated with more than one customer, so the composite relationship key must be chosen with care.
questions.visualHook: Use the schema-diagram key chooser for the bank example.

questions.prompt: Sketch the schema diagram for the bank database: which relations appear and which foreign-key edges are drawn between them?
accepted: branch, customer, account, loan, depositor, borrower with FK edges
keys underlined and relationships by foreign keys
questions.solution: The diagram shows branch, customer, account, loan, depositor, and borrower with primary keys connected: account references branch, depositor references customer and account, borrower references customer and loan, and loan references branch. Foreign-key edges map the referential relationships.
questions.explanation: A schema diagram is a visual map of relation attributes plus the referential-integrity edges that connect them.
questions.misconception: Do not read the diagram as data; it encodes structure and key relationships.
questions.visualHook: Inspect the figure schema_diagram_2_13.png for the actual bank diagram.

questions.prompt: Write a relational-algebra expression that returns each loan number with a loan amount greater than USD 10,000 in the bank database.
accepted: Pi_loan_number (sigma_amount > 10000 (loan))
project loan_number from loan filtered by amount
questions.solution: Select loan rows whose amount exceeds USD 10,000, then project loan_number. The selection filters the loan relation; the projection keeps only the attribute needed in the answer.
questions.explanation: Select filters rows by predicate; project drops the attributes not needed in the answer.
questions.misconception: Select and project act on different parts of the expression: filter rows then choose columns.
questions.visualHook: Run this expression through the algebra pipeline in the lab.

questions.prompt: Write an SQL query to find the titles of all courses in the Comp. Sci. department that have 3 credits.
accepted: SELECT title FROM course WHERE dept_name = 'Comp. Sci.' AND credits = 3
questions.solution: Project the title column from course, restricting rows to the Comp. Sci. department and to courses carrying three credits.
questions.explanation: The where clause filters the course rows by department and credits before projection returns only the title column.
questions.misconception: Composite predicates combine naturally with AND after select-from-where.
questions.visualHook: Trace the select-from-where order in the SQL flow visual.

questions.prompt: Write the SQL statement that increases the salary of each instructor in the Comp. Sci. department by 10%.
accepted: UPDATE instructor SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE dept_name = 'Comp. Sci.'
questions.solution: Update instructor rows in the Comp. Sci. department by multiplying each selected salary by 1.10.
questions.explanation: UPDATE modifies existing tuples; the WHERE restricts which instructor rows are changed.
questions.misconception: Without a WHERE clause the update would apply to every instructor row.
questions.visualHook: Watch the UPDATE pipeline only touch Comp. Sci. rows.

questions.prompt: Write an SQL query that finds departments whose names contain the substring "sci", regardless of case.
accepted: SELECT dept_name FROM department WHERE LOWER(dept_name) LIKE '%sci%'
questions.solution: Normalize dept_name with LOWER and apply a pattern that contains the substring sci.
questions.explanation: LIKE performs pattern matching; LOWER normalizes the column value so the match is case-insensitive.
questions.misconception: LIKE alone is case sensitive in most systems; LOWER is what makes the match case-insensitive.
questions.visualHook: Compare LIKE versus LOWER(LIKE) in the string-operations lab.

questions.prompt: Using the university schema, write an SQL query that finds the lowest, across all departments, of the per-department maximum instructor salary.
accepted: SELECT MIN(max_salary) FROM (SELECT MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM instructor GROUP BY dept_name)
single-query aggregation of per-department maximum
questions.solution: Compute each department's maximum instructor salary in an inner grouped query, then take the minimum of those maxima in an outer query.
questions.explanation: The inner query computes each department's maximum; the outer MIN aggregates those maxima to find the lowest one.
questions.misconception: You cannot take MIN of MAX in one flat group-by; a nesting is required.
questions.visualHook: Follow the nested aggregation in the group-by lab.

questions.prompt: Using a WITH clause, write an SQL query to find the IDs of students who have retaken at least three distinct courses at least once (course taken at least two times).
accepted: WITH repeated_courses AS (SELECT ID, course_id FROM takes GROUP BY ID, course_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2) SELECT ID FROM repeated_courses GROUP BY ID HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
GROUP BY id having count of repeated course_ids at least 3
questions.solution: Use a common table expression to keep student-course pairs that occur more than once, then group by student and retain students with at least three repeated courses.
questions.explanation: The CTE keeps only course-student pairs taken more than once; the outer group counts how many repeated courses each student has, keeping those with at least three.
questions.misconception: The inner HAVING keeps repeated courses, while the outer HAVING keeps students with enough repeated courses.
questions.visualHook: Inspect the two-level HAVING in the CTE lab.

questions.prompt: Write an SQL query using NOT EXISTS to find the names and IDs of instructors who teach every course taught in their own department, ordered by name.
accepted: NOT EXISTS with course EXCEPT teaches
division query against department's course set
questions.solution: For each instructor, take the set difference between the department's course set and the instructor's taught-course set; keep instructors for whom that difference is empty, and order by name.
questions.explanation: For each instructor, the EXCEPT removes the courses they actually teach from the set of their department's courses; NOT EXISTS keeps instructors for whom no leftover course is not taught.
questions.misconception: Division by all-courses requires set difference with NOT EXISTS, not a simple equal-all comparison.
questions.visualHook: Use the categorical division visual for this pattern.

questions.prompt: A new row is inserted into instructor without changing its table definition. What changed?
choices: The relation schema
The relation instance
The primary-key definition
The attribute domain
questions.explanation: An instance is the current set of tuples; inserting a row changes that state while the schema remains the same.
questions.misconception: Schema describes structure; it is not the current collection of rows.
questions.visualHook: Compare the stable relation schema with the changing table snapshot.

questions.prompt: For Enrollment(student_id, course_id, term, grade), assume one student can take a course once per term. State a minimal candidate key and explain why it is minimal.
accepted: student_id course_id term is the composite candidate key
student_id, course_id, and term uniquely identify an enrollment
the three-attribute composite key
questions.solution: A minimal candidate key is the combination of student_id, course_id, and term. Removing any one attribute allows two different enrollments to share the remaining values.
questions.explanation: The key encodes the business rule that a student-course pair may repeat across terms but not within the same term.
questions.misconception: student_id alone is not unique because one student can enroll in many courses and terms.
questions.visualHook: Test uniqueness and minimality by removing one attribute at a time.

questions.prompt: Which relational-algebra operator keeps rows satisfying a predicate while preserving the relation's attributes?
choices: Selection
Projection
Rename
Union
questions.explanation: Selection filters tuples by a predicate; projection chooses attributes and therefore changes the output schema.
questions.misconception: Relational selection is a row filter, not the column list written after SQL SELECT.
questions.visualHook: Toggle the row-filter and column-filter views side by side.

questions.prompt: Write the relational-algebra construction for instructors and teaches that retains only matching instructor identifiers, then explain why the unfiltered product is insufficient.
accepted: selection on instructor.ID = teaches.ID over instructor cross teaches
join equals product followed by selection
theta join with matching IDs
questions.solution: Use a theta join on the identifier condition. Equivalently, apply selection with the matching instructor and teaches identifiers to the Cartesian product. The raw product contains every possible pair, including unrelated instructor-course pairs.
questions.explanation: The join predicate is the semantic link; without it, the product creates false associations.
questions.misconception: A Cartesian product combines rows mechanically; it does not infer a relationship.
questions.visualHook: Inspect how the matching predicate removes false tuple pairs.

questions.prompt: Which condition is required before applying union to two relations?
choices: They must have equal row counts
They must have equal arity and compatible corresponding domains
They must share a primary key name
They must be joined first
questions.explanation: Union is defined for compatible relation schemas: the operands need the same number of attributes and compatible domains in corresponding positions.
questions.misconception: Union compatibility is about tuple shape and domains, not equal row counts.
questions.visualHook: Check operand compatibility before combining the tuple sets.

questions.prompt: Explain why the queries Fall minus Spring and Spring minus Fall are generally different.
accepted: set difference is directional
left operand is retained and right operand is subtracted
difference is not commutative
questions.solution: Set difference keeps tuples in its left operand that do not occur in its right operand, so reversing the operands reverses which semester's exclusive courses are returned.
questions.explanation: Unlike union and intersection, set difference is order-sensitive.
questions.misconception: Do not assume every set operator is commutative.
questions.visualHook: Swap the operands and watch the exclusive set change.

questions.prompt: Why is rename needed when finding instructors who earn more than instructor 12121? Describe the two relation roles.
accepted: rename creates a second named copy for self-comparison
one instructor reference is compared with a renamed instructor reference
self-join requires two aliases
questions.solution: Rename creates a second name for the instructor relation so one reference can represent the candidate instructor and the other can represent instructor 12121. The query can then compare their salaries.
questions.explanation: The base relation is used twice in different logical roles; aliases make those roles distinguishable.
questions.misconception: Rename does not duplicate stored data; it gives an expression or relation reference a second name.
questions.visualHook: Label the candidate and benchmark copies before writing the predicate.

questions.prompt: When can two different relational-algebra expressions be called equivalent?
accepted: they return the same result for every database instance
same relation on every database
equivalent expressions preserve the logical result
questions.solution: They are equivalent when they produce the same relation for every possible database instance, even if their intermediate relations or operation order differ.
questions.explanation: Equivalence is a semantic guarantee across all database states, not an accidental match on one sample.
questions.misconception: A query that matches one test dataset is not proven equivalent.
questions.visualHook: Compare two expressions across multiple relation instances.

questions.prompt: What anomaly can occur when instructor and department are stored in one wide relation and the department building is repeated across instructor rows?
accepted: update anomaly
repeated department facts can become inconsistent
redundancy causes update insertion and deletion anomalies
questions.solution: An update anomaly can create contradictory building values for the same department when only some repeated copies are changed. The repetition can also create insertion and deletion anomalies.
questions.explanation: The lecture uses the wide natural-join relation as a preview of why decomposition and normalization matter.
questions.misconception: Fewer tables do not automatically mean less redundancy or better integrity.
questions.visualHook: Highlight repeated department facts and edit only one copy.

questions.prompt: Which statement changes the schema rather than only the current relation instance?
choices: INSERT INTO instructor (ID, name, dept_name, salary) VALUES (12345, 'Lee', 'Comp. Sci.', 80000)
DELETE FROM instructor
ALTER TABLE instructor ADD office varchar(20)
UPDATE assigns new tuple values
questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE changes the relation definition; the other statements operate on tuples.
questions.misconception: Separate schema-changing DDL from tuple-changing DML.
questions.visualHook: Toggle the schema layer and the current-instance layer.

questions.prompt: Write an SQL query that returns the names of Computer Science instructors whose salary is above 70,000. Explain the role of each clause.
accepted: select name from instructor where dept_name = Comp. Sci. and salary > 70000
SELECT name FROM instructor WHERE dept_name = 'Comp. Sci.' AND salary > 70000
select name, from instructor, where department and salary predicate
questions.solution: Return name from instructor after filtering for the Computer Science department and salary above 70,000. SELECT supplies the output, FROM supplies the relation, and WHERE applies the row predicate.
questions.explanation: The query tests the basic query shape and combines two row predicates with AND.
questions.misconception: Do not put the salary condition in SELECT or omit the relation source in FROM.
questions.visualHook: Build the query by arranging output, source, and predicate tokens.

questions.prompt: When should SELECT DISTINCT be added?
choices: When every source row must be preserved
When duplicate projected result rows must be removed
When a table schema must change
When a foreign key must be deferred
questions.explanation: SQL keeps duplicates by default; DISTINCT requests duplicate elimination in the projected result.
questions.misconception: Do not assume SQL has pure set semantics by default.
questions.visualHook: Compare SELECT ALL and SELECT DISTINCT on the same result.

questions.prompt: Why is FROM instructor, teaches alone insufficient to identify which instructor taught which course?
accepted: it creates a Cartesian product
every instructor is paired with every teaches row
a key equality predicate is required
join on instructor.ID and teaches.ID
questions.solution: The FROM clause creates all possible instructor-teaches pairs. A WHERE predicate matching instructor.ID with teaches.ID is needed to retain only related pairs.
questions.explanation: A multi-table query needs an explicit relationship predicate; row position is not identity.
questions.misconception: Listing two relations does not automatically establish their relationship.
questions.visualHook: Show the product first, then animate the key predicate filtering it.

questions.prompt: For each course section offered in 2017, find the average total credits of enrolled students only when the section has at least two students. Which clause receives the row predicate and which receives the aggregate predicate?
accepted: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY and HAVING filters groups after aggregation
GROUP BY section and HAVING COUNT >= 2
WHERE year = 2017, GROUP BY section, HAVING count(student.ID) >= 2
questions.solution: Use WHERE for row-level restrictions such as the target year, GROUP BY for course and section identity, and HAVING for the minimum group-size threshold. The average belongs in SELECT.
questions.explanation: The BIG 6 is a semantic pipeline: row filtering precedes grouping, while HAVING sees completed groups.
questions.misconception: An aggregate predicate cannot be evaluated at the row-filtering stage.
questions.visualHook: Trace rows through WHERE, groups through GROUP BY, and survivors through HAVING.

questions.prompt: Which predicate correctly finds instructors whose salary is missing?
choices: ordinary comparison with NULL
salary IS NULL
programming-style equality with NULL
salary is equal to zero
questions.explanation: NULL requires IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; ordinary comparison with NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN.
questions.misconception: NULL is not an ordinary value and is not the same as zero.
questions.visualHook: Run an ordinary NULL comparison and IS NULL side by side.

questions.prompt: A column contains the values 40, NULL, and 60. What do COUNT(column) and COUNT(*) return for these three rows?
accepted: COUNT(column) is 2 and COUNT(*) is 3
2 and 3
count ignores null values but count star counts rows
questions.solution: COUNT(column) returns 2 because NULL is ignored for that column; COUNT(*) returns 3 because it counts rows.
questions.explanation: The distinction is essential when aggregates meet missing values.
questions.misconception: COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) do not have the same NULL behavior.
questions.visualHook: Highlight the NULL cell and compare the two counters.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL in SQL?
accepted: UNION removes duplicates and UNION ALL preserves duplicates
UNION distinct, UNION ALL bag semantics
all keeps duplicate rows
questions.solution: UNION combines compatible query results and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL combines them while retaining duplicates.
questions.explanation: Set-operation syntax controls whether duplicate result tuples are preserved.
questions.misconception: Do not assume every set-looking SQL operator removes duplicates.
questions.visualHook: Overlay two semester result sets with and without deduplication.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between SOME and ALL in a salary comparison against a subquery result.
accepted: SOME is existential and needs one witness
ALL is universal and needs every value
one counterexample defeats ALL
questions.solution: x greater-than SOME(Q) succeeds if x is greater than at least one value in Q. x greater-than ALL(Q) succeeds only if x is greater than every value in Q.
questions.explanation: SOME and ALL quantify over the values returned by the subquery; they are not interchangeable.
questions.misconception: Do not use SOME when the requirement is a universal maximum-style condition.
questions.visualHook: Reveal one witness for SOME and search for a counterexample to ALL.

questions.prompt: How does the NOT EXISTS pattern express that a student took every course offered by the Biology department?
accepted: find no Biology course missing from the student's takes rows
required courses minus taken courses is empty
not exists a counterexample
questions.solution: For each student, form the required Biology courses and subtract the courses that student took. Keep the student only when no required course remains missing.
questions.explanation: Universal requirements are often easiest to implement as the absence of a counterexample.
questions.misconception: A simple equality compares one value; this requirement compares two sets.
questions.visualHook: Show the required set minus the student set and keep only empty differences.

questions.prompt: Why is a common table expression useful for a multi-step SQL query?
accepted: it names a temporary relation
it improves readability without changing stored data
WITH makes intermediate results explicit
questions.solution: WITH names a temporary relation for the duration of one statement, allowing later parts of the query to refer to a readable intermediate result.
questions.explanation: A CTE exposes intermediate reasoning without creating a permanent table.
questions.misconception: A CTE is statement-scoped, not a permanent schema object.
questions.visualHook: Expand a nested query into named CTE stages.

questions.prompt: What is the safety role of WHERE in UPDATE and DELETE statements?
accepted: WHERE determines which tuples are mutated
without WHERE all rows are affected
SET changes values and WHERE identifies target rows
questions.solution: WHERE defines the mutation set. Without it, UPDATE changes every row and DELETE removes every tuple in the target relation, subject to constraint behavior.
questions.explanation: DML syntax is short, but the predicate determines the scope of a potentially destructive operation.
questions.misconception: SET changes values; it does not select the rows to mutate.
questions.visualHook: Preview the mutation set before applying UPDATE or DELETE.

questions.prompt: List six major steps for setting up a database for a particular enterprise.
accepted: requirements, data model, integrity constraints, physical design, applications, initialization
define requirements and model, constraints, physical level, interfaces and applications, initialize database
questions.solution: Define the enterprise requirements; define the data model and relationships; define integrity constraints; define the physical level; design the required user interfaces and applications; then create and initialize the database.
questions.explanation: Database setup moves from enterprise requirements and logical meaning to constraints, physical choices, applications, and initialization.
questions.misconception: Database setup is not only creating tables; requirements, integrity, physical design, and applications are part of the lifecycle.
questions.visualHook: Arrange the six steps on a requirements-to-initialization pipeline.

questions.prompt: List four significant differences between a file-processing system and a DBMS.
accepted: generality, atomicity, concurrency control, authorization
DBMS is more general and provides transaction, concurrency, and access-control support
questions.solution: A file-processing system is usually problem-specific, while a DBMS is general-purpose. A DBMS also makes atomic updates, protection from concurrent-access anomalies, and per-user authorization substantially easier to enforce.
questions.explanation: The comparison tests why a DBMS is a system with shared guarantees rather than merely a collection of files.
questions.misconception: A file format alone does not provide transaction atomicity, concurrency protection, or database authorization.
questions.visualHook: Compare the guarantees available in a file-processing stack and a DBMS stack.

questions.prompt: Give at least two reasons database systems use a declarative query language such as SQL instead of only C or C++ data-manipulation functions.
accepted: declarative languages are easier to learn and use
declarative logic leaves physical algorithms and optimization to the DBMS
questions.solution: Declarative queries are easier to learn and use for stating what data is wanted. They also let users work at the logical level while the DBMS selects efficient physical algorithms and access paths.
questions.explanation: SQL separates the desired result from the physical procedure used to obtain it.
questions.misconception: Declarative SQL does not require users to hand-code the physical execution algorithm for each query.
questions.visualHook: Trace one declarative query from logical intent to an optimizer-selected physical plan.

questions.prompt: Describe at least three tables that might store information in a social-networking system such as Facebook.
accepted: users, chats, friends
user table, conversation table, friendship table
questions.solution: A simple design could include Users for identity and profile attributes, Chats for conversations, and Friends for pairs of user IDs representing relationships between users.
questions.explanation: The exercise turns an application domain into candidate entities and relationships that can later be modeled and constrained.
questions.misconception: A table design should represent distinct entities or relationships rather than putting every kind of social data into one table.
questions.visualHook: Sketch Users, Chats, and Friends as connected tables with their key relationships.

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

This chapter has described several major advantages of a database system. What are two disadvantages?
questions.solution:
Two disadvantages associated with database systems are listed below.
* Setup of the database system requires more knowledge, money, skills, and time. 
* The complexity of the database may result in poor performance.
questions.explanation: MCQ adaptation of the teacher-assigned exercise (original response type: short). The correct option is a concise solution summary; open the worked solution below to study the exact SQL, design, or derivation.
questions.misconception: Do not copy the final answer without checking the assumptions, intermediate steps, and required constraints.
questions.visualHook: Write the entities, operators, clauses, or dependency steps on a small scratch diagram before checking the solution.
choices: Examples include Google Maps, Facebook, Medium, and Bitcoin.
Two disadvantages are the cost and complexity of setting up a DBMS, and the risk that this complexity hurts performance.
There are 3 levels of data abstraction in a database: Physical Level, Logical Level and View Level.
A DBMS provides security, atomicity, efficient queries, durability, and concurrency control; without them data may be exposed, inconsistent, lost, or stale.

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

List five ways in which the type declaration system of a language such as Java or C++ differs from the
data definition language used in a database.
questions.solution:
a. Executing an action in the DDL results in the creation of an object in the 
database; in contrast, a programming language type declaration is simply an 
abstraction used in the program. 

b. Database DDLs allow consistency constraints to be specified, which programming
language type systems generally do not allow. These include domain constraints and
referential integrity constraints. 

c. Database DDLs support authorization, giving different access rights to 
different users. Programming language type systems do not provide such 
protection (at best, they protect attributes in a class from being accessed
by methods in another class).

d. Programming language type systems are usually much richer than the SQL 
type system. Most databases support only basic types such as different types
of numbers and strings, although some databases do support some complex types 
such as arrays and objects. 

e. A database DDL is focused on specifying types of attributes of relations;
in contrast, a programming language allows objects and collections of objects
to be created.

List six major steps that you would take in setting up a database for a particular enterprise.
questions.solution:
Six major steps in setting up a database for a particular enterprise are:

* Define the high-level requirements of the enterprise (this step generates a 
document known as the system requirements specification). 

* Define a model containing all appropriate types of data and data relationships. 

* Define the integrity constraints on the data. 

* Define the physical level. 

* For each known problem to be solved on a regular basis (e.g., tasks to be
carried out by clerks or web users), define a user interface to carry out the
task, and write the necessary application programs to implement the user interface. 

* Create/initialize the database.

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

Suppose you want to build a video site similar to YouTube. Consider each of the 
points listed in Section 1.2 as disadvantages of keeping data in a file-processing 
system. Discuss the relevance of each of these points to the storage of actual 
video data, and to metadata about the video, such as title, the user who uploaded it, 
tags, and which users viewed it.
questions.solution:
* Data redundancy and inconsistency: This would be relevant to metadata to some extent, 
although not to the actual video data, which are not updated. There are very few relationships
here, and none of them can lead to redundancy. 

* Difficulty in accessing data: If video data are only accessed through a few predefined 
interfaces, as is done in video sharing sites today, this will not be a problem. However, if an 
organization needs to find video data based on specific search conditions (beyond simple
keyword queries), if metadata were stored in files it would be hard to find relevant data
without writing application programs. Using a database would be important for the task of finding
data. 

* Data isolation: Since data are not usually updated, but instead newly created, 
data isolation is not a major issue. Even the task of keeping track of who has viewed what
videos is (conceptually) append only, again making isolation not a major issue. 
However, if authorization is added, there may be some issues of concurrent updates
to authorization information. 

* Integrity Problems: It seems unlikely there are significant integrity 
constraints in this application, except for primary keys. If the data are 
distributed there may be issues in enforcing primary key constraints. Integrity
problems are probably not a major issue. 

* Atomicity problems: When a video is uploaded, metadata about the video 
and the video should be added atomically, otherwise there would be an inconsistency
in the data. An underlying recovery mechanism would be required to ensure atomicity
in the event of failures. 

* Concurrent-access anomalies: Since data are not updated, concurrent access anomalies
would be unlikely to occur. 

* Security problems: These would be an issue if the system supported authorization.

List four significant differences between a file-processing system and a DBMS.
questions.solution:
1) A file-processing system is more specific to the problem at hand while a DBMS
is more general. A file-processing system used by a university is difficult to 
use in a hospital setting. While a DBMS once written can be used in different places. 

2) It is difficult to ensure atomicity in a conventional file-processing system while
it is a lot easier in a DBMS. Often wrapping a set of SQL statements in a "BEGIN TRANSACTION"
and "END TRANSACTION" are often enough in the relational DBMS world. 

3) Protecting against concurrent-access anomalies in a file-processing system is 
difficult. Using a DBMS is much easier to protect against concurrent-access anomalies.

4) Most DBMS have a concept of a user and what access that user has. Enforcing such 
authorization in a file-processing system is really difficult.

questions.prompt:

Explain the difference between two-tier and three-tier application architectures.
Which is better suited for web applications? Why?
questions.solution:
* Earlier-generation database applications used a two-tier architecture, where as
a three-tier architecture is used by a modern database application. 

* In a two-tier architecture the application resides at the client machine, and invokes
database system functionality at the server machine through query language statements. 
In a three-tier architecture the client machine acts as merely a front end and 
does not contain any direct database calls ; the front end communicates with an 
application server. The application server, in turn, communicates with a database
system to access data. 

* Three-tier applications provide better security as well as better performance
than two-tier applications. 

Note: Even though the book classifies database applications in to two, the reality is 
that most famous applications use four-tier architecture. If we take most chatting
mobile applications they are a three-tier architecture with a local database
such as sqlite for caching the data and accessing it when the mobile is not connected
to the internet.

questions.prompt:
Consider the employee database of Figure 2.17. Give an expression in the relational
algebra to express each of the following queries: 
a. Find the ID and name of each employee who does not work for "BigBank. 

b. Find the ID and name of each employee who earns at least as much as 
every employee in the database.
questions.solution:
a. To find employees who do not work for BigBank, we first find all those
who do work for BigBank. Those are exactly the employees not part of the 
desired result. We then use set difference to find the set of all employees minus
those employees that should not be in the result. 

$\Pi_{ID, person\_name}(employee) - \Pi_{ID, person\_name}(
    employee \bowtie_{employee.ID = works.ID} (\sigma_{company\_name="BigBank"}(works))
)$ 

b. We use the same approach as in part a by first finding those employees
who do not earn the highest salary, or, said differently, for whom some other
employees earns more. Since this involves comparing two employee salary values, 
we need to reference the employee relation twice and therefore use renaming. 

$\Pi_{ID, person\_name}(employee) - \Pi_{A.ID, A.person\_name}(\rho_A(employee) 
\bowtie_{A.salary < B.salary} \rho_B(employee))$

Comment: This is the answer that is provided here. But if you look at Figure 2.17 closely the employee
relation doesn't have an attribute called salary.

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

The division operator of relational algebra, "$\div$" is defined as follows. 
Let $r(R)$ and $s(S)$ be relations, and let $S \subseteq R$; that is, every attribute
of schema $S$ is also in schema $R$. Given a tuple $t$, let $t[S]$ denote the projection
of tuple $t$ on the attributes in $S$. Then $r \div s$ is a relation on schema $R - S$ 
(that is, on the schema containing all attributes of schema $R$ that are not in schema $S$). 
A tuple $t$ is in $r \div s$ if and only if both of two conditions hold: 
* $t$ is in $\Pi_{R-S}(r)$
* For every tuple $t_s$ in $s$, there is a tuple $t_r$ in $r$ satisfying both of the
following: 

    a. $t_r[S] = t_s[S]$ 

    b. $t_r[R - S] = t$ 

Given the above definition: 

a. Write a relational algebra expression using the division operator to find 
the IDs of all students who have taken all Comp. Sci. courses. (Hint: project takes 
to just ID and course_id, and generate the set of all Comp. Sci. course_id s using 
a select expression, before doing the division.)

 
b. Show how to write the above query in relational algebra, without using division. 
(By doing so, you would have shown how to define the division operation using the other 
relational algebra operations.)
questions.solution:
a. $\Pi_{ID,course\_id}(takes) \div \Pi_{course\_id}(\sigma_{dept\_name = 'Comp. Sci'}(course))$

b. The required expression is as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}
    r \leftarrow \Pi_{ID,course\_id}(takes) \\\\
    s \leftarrow \Pi_{course\_id}(\sigma_{dept\_name = 'Comp. Sci'}(course)) \\\\
    \Pi_{ID}(takes) - \Pi_{ID}((\Pi_{ID}(takes) \times s) - r)
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, let $r(R)$ and $s(S)$ be given, with $S \subseteq R$. Then we 
can express the division operation using basic relational algebra operations 
as follows: 
$$
    r \div s = \Pi_{R-S}(r) - \Pi_{R-S}((\Pi_{R-S}(r) \times s) - \Pi_{R-S, S}(r))
$$

To see that this expression is true, we observe that $\Pi_{R-S}(r)$ gives us all 
tuples $t$ that satisfy the first condition of the definition of division. The expression
on the right side of the set difference operator
$
    \Pi_{R-S}((\Pi_{R-S}(r) \times s) - \Pi_{R-S, S}(r))
$
serves to eliminate those tuples that fail to satisfy the second condition of the 
definition of division. Let us see how it does so. Consider $\Pi_{R-S}(r) \times s$.
This relation is on schema $R$, and pairs every tuple in $\Pi_{R-S}(r)$ with 
every tuple in $s$. The expression $\Pi_{R-S,S}(r)$ merely reorders the attributes 
of $r$. 

Thus, $(\Pi_{R-S}(r) \times s) - \Pi_{R-S, S}(r)$ gives us those pairs of tuples
from $\Pi_{R-S}(r)$ and $s$ that do not appear in $r$. If a tuple $t_j$ is in 
$
    \Pi_{R-S}((\Pi_{R-S}(r) \times s) - \Pi_{R-S, S}(r))
$
then there is some tuple $t_s$ in $s$ that does not combine with tuple $t_j$
to form a tuple in $r$. Thus, $t_j$ holds a value for attributes $R - S$ that does
not appear in $r \div s$. It is these values that we eliminate from $\Pi_{R-S}(r)$.

Consider the employee database of Figure 2.17. Give an expression 
in the relational algebra to express each of the following queries: 

a. Find the ID and name of each employee who works for "BigBank". 

b. Find the ID, name, and city of residence of each employee who 
works for "BigBank". 

c. Find the ID, name, street address, and city of residence of 
each employee who works for "BigBank" and earns more than USD 10000. 

d. Find the ID and name of each employee in this database who lives 
in the same city as the company for which she or he works.
questions.solution:
We assume that there is an ID attribute on the employee relation.

We also assume that the attributes person_name and company_name are UNIQUE in the relations
employee and company respectively. 

a. $$\Pi_{ID, person\_name}(employee \bowtie_{employee.person\_name = works.person\_name} \sigma_{company\_name="BigBank"}(works))$$

b. $$\Pi_{ID, person\_name, city}(employee \bowtie_{employee.person\_name = works.person\_name} \sigma_{company\_name="BigBank"}(works))$$

c. $$\Pi_{ID, person\_name, street, city}(employee \bowtie_{employee.person\_name = works.person\_name} \sigma_{company\_name="BigBank" \wedge salary > 10000 }(works))$$

d. 

Method 1: 

$$S1 \leftarrow (company \bowtie_{company.company\_name = works.company\_name} works)$$

$$\Pi_{ID, person\_name} (S1 \bowtie_{S1.person\_name = employee.person\_name \wedge S1.city = employee.city} employee))$$

Method 2: 

$$\Pi_{ID, person\_name}(employee \bowtie_{employee.person\_name = works.person\_name} works \bowtie_{works.company\_name = company.company\_name \wedge employee.city = company.city} company)$$

questions.prompt:
Write the following queries in SQL, using the university schema. (We suggest
you actually run these queries on a database, using the sample data that we 
provide on the website of the book, db-book.com. Instructions for setting up 
a database, and loading sample data, are provided on the above website.)

a. Find the titles of courses in the Comp. Sci. department that have 3 credits. 

b. Find the IDs of all students who were taught by an instructor named Einstein;
make sure there are no duplicates in the result. 

c. Find the highest salary of any instructor. 

d. Find all instructors earning the highest salary (there may be more than one with 
the same salary). 

e. Find the enrollment of each section that was offered in Fall 2017. 
 
f. Find the maximum enrollment, across all sections, in Fall 2017. 

g. Find the sections that had the maximum enrollment in Fall 2017.
questions.solution:
a. Find the titles of courses in the Comp. Sci. department that have 3 credits. 

```sql
SELECT title 
FROM course
WHERE dept_name = 'Comp. Sci.' AND credits = 3;
```

b. Find the IDs of all students who were taught by an instructor named Einstein;
make sure there are no duplicates in the result.
This query can be answered in several different ways. One way is as follows. 

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT takes.ID
FROM takes, instructor, teaches
WHERE takes.course_id = teaches.course_id AND 
    takes.sec_id = teaches.sec_id AND 
    takes.semester = teaches.semester AND 
    takes.year = teaches.year AND 
    teaches.id = instructor.id AND 
    instructor.name = 'Einstein'
```

Another method by using subqueries 

```sql 
SELECT DISTINCT id 
FROM takes
WHERE (course_id, sec_id, semester, year) IN 
(
    SELECT course_id, sec_id, semester, year 
    FROM teaches INNER JOIN instructor 
        ON teaches.id = instructor.id
    WHERE instructor.name = 'Einstein'
);
```

c. Find the highest salary of any instructor.

```sql 
SELECT MAX(salary) 
FROM instructor
```

d. Find all instructors earning the highest salary (there may be more than one with 
the same salary).

```sql
SELECT id, name
FROM instructor
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM instructor)
```

e. Find the enrollment of each section that was offered in Fall 2017.

```sql
SELECT course_id, sec_id, (
    SELECT COUNT(id)
    FROM takes
    WHERE takes.year = section.year
        AND takes.semester = section.semester
        AND takes.course_id = section.course_id 
        AND takes.sec_id = section.sec_id
) AS enrollment 
FROM section 
WHERE semester = 'Fall' AND year = 2017
```

Note that if the result of the subquery is empty, the aggregate function 
count returns a value of 0. One way of writing the query might appear 
to be: 

```sql
SELECT course_id, sec_id, COUNT(id)
FROM takes
WHERE semester = 'Fall' AND year = 2017
GROUP BY course_id, sec_id
```

But note that if a section does not have any students taking it, it would 
not appear in the result. One way of ensuring such a section appears with 
a count of 0 is to use the outer join operation, covered in Chapter 4. 

f. Find the maximum enrollment, across all sections, in Fall 2017.
One way of writing this query is as follows: 

```sql 
WITH enrollment_in_fall_2017(course_id, sec_id, enrollment) AS (
    SELECT course_id, sec_id, COUNT(id)
    FROM takes
    WHERE semester = 'Fall' AND year = 2017
    GROUP BY course_id, sec_id
) 
SELECT CASE 
        WHEN MAX(enrollment) IS NOT NULL THEN MAX(enrollment)
        ELSE 0
       END
FROM enrollment_in_fall_2017;
```

g. Find the sections that had the maximum enrollment in Fall 2017.

```sql 
WITH enrollment_in_fall_2017(course_id, sec_id, enrollment) AS (
    SELECT course_id, sec_id, COUNT(id) 
    FROM takes
    WHERE semester = 'Fall' AND year = 2017
    GROUP BY course_id, sec_id
) 
SELECT course_id, sec_id
FROM enrollment_in_fall_2017
WHERE enrollment = (SELECT MAX(enrollment) FROM enrollment_in_fall_2017);
```

It is also possible to write the query without the with clause, 
but the subquery to find enrollment would get repeated twice in the query. While
not incorrect to add distinct in the count, it is not necessary in light
of the primary key constraint on takes.

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

Suppose you are given a relation grade_points(grade, points) that provides
a conversion from letter grades in the takes relation to numeric scores; for example, 
an "A" grade could be specified to correspond to 4 points, an "A-" to 3.7 points, 
a "B+" to 3.3 points, a "B" to 3 points and so on. The grade points earned by a 
student for a course offering (section) is defined as the number of credits for 
the course multiplied by the numeric points for the grade that the student received. 

Given the preceding relation and our university schema, write each of the following 
queries in SQL. You may assume for simplicity that no takes tuple has the null
value for grade. 

a. Find the total grade points earned by the student with ID '12345', across
all courses taken by the student. 

b. Find the grade point average (GPA) for the above student, that is, the total 
grade points divided by the total credits for the associated courses. 

c. Find the ID and the grade-point average of each student. 

d. Now reconsider your answers to the earlier parts of this exercise under the assumption
that some grades might be null. Explain whether your solutions still work and, if not, 
provide versions that handle nulls properly.
questions.solution:
a. Find the total grade points earned by the student with ID '12345', across
all courses taken by the student.

```sql 
SELECT SUM(c.credits * g.points)
FROM takes AS t 
    INNER JOIN course AS c ON t.course_id = c.course_id
    INNER JOIN grade_points AS g ON t.grade = g.grade
WHERE t.ID = '12345'
```

In the above query, a student who has not taken any course would not
have any tuples, whereas we would expect to get 0 as the answer. One 
way of fixing this problem is to use the outer join operation, which 
we study later in Chapter 4. Another way to ensure that we get 0 as the answer 
is via the following query: 

```sql
(
SELECT SUM(c.credits * g.points)
FROM takes AS t 
    INNER JOIN course AS c ON t.course_id = c.course_id
    INNER JOIN grade_points AS g ON t.grade = g.grade
WHERE t.ID = '12345'
)
UNION 
(
SELECT 0
FROM student 
WHERE ID = '12345' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM takes WHERE ID = '12345')
)
```

b. Find the grade point average (GPA) for the above student, that is, the total 
grade-points divided by the total credits for the associated courses.

```sql 
SELECT SUM(c.credits * g.points) / SUM(credits) AS GPA
FROM takes AS t 
    INNER JOIN course AS c ON t.course_id = c.course_id
    INNER JOIN grade_points AS g ON t.grade = g.grade
WHERE t.ID = '12345'
```

As before, a student who has not taken any course would not appear in the 
above result; we can ensure that such a student appears in the result by 
using the modified query from the previous part of this question. However, 
an additional issue in this case is that the sum of credits would also be 0, 
resulting in a divide-by-zero condition. In fact, the only meaningful way of 
defining the GPA in this case is to define it as null. We can ensure that 
such a student appears in the result with a null GPA by adding the following
union clause to the above query. 

```sql
UNION 
(
    SELECT null AS GPA 
    FROM student 
    WHERE ID = '12345' AND 
        NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM takes WHERE ID='12345')
)
```

c. Find the ID and the grade-point average of each student.

```sql 
SELECT t.ID, SUM(c.credits * g.points) / SUM(credits) AS GPA
FROM takes AS t 
    INNER JOIN course AS c ON t.course_id = c.course_id
    INNER JOIN grade_points AS g ON t.grade = g.grade
GROUP BY t.ID
```

Again, to handle students who have not taken any course, we would have
to add the following union clause:

```sql 
UNION 
(
    SELECT ID, null AS GPA 
    FROM student 
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM takes WHERE takes.ID = student.ID)
)
```

d. Now reconsider your answers to the earlier parts of this exercise under the assumption
that some grades might be null. Explain whether your solutions still work and, if not, 
provide versions that handle nulls properly.

The queries listed above all include a test of equality on grade between
grade_points and takes. Thus, for any takes tuple with a null grade, 
that student's course would be eliminated from the rest of the computation 
of the result. As a result, the credits of such courses would be eliminated 
also, and thus the queries would return the correct answer even if some grades
are null.

questions.solution:

FROM accident, participated, person, owns

      AND owns.driver_id = person.driver_id

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

Suppose that we have a relation marks(ID,score) and we wish to assign grades
to students based on the score as follows: grade F if score $<$ 40, grade C
if 40 $\leq$ score $<$ 60, grade B if 60 $\leq$ score $<$ 80, and grade A
if 80 $\leq$ score. Write SQL queries to do the following: 

a. Display the grade for each student, based on the marks relation. 

b. Find the number of students with each grade.
questions.solution:
a. Display the grade for each student, based on the marks relation.

```sql
SELECT ID, 
    CASE
        WHEN score < 40 THEN 'F'
        WHEN score < 60 THEN 'C'
        WHEN score < 80 THEN 'B'
        ELSE 'A' 
    END
FROM marks
```

b. Find the number of students with each grade.

```sql
WITH grades(ID,grade) AS (
    SELECT ID, 
        CASE
            WHEN score < 40 THEN 'F'
            WHEN score < 60 THEN 'C'
            WHEN score < 80 THEN 'B'
            ELSE 'A' 
        END
    FROM marks
) 
SELECT grade, COUNT(ID)
FROM grades
GROUP BY grade
```

As an alternative, the WITH clause can be removed, and instead the 
definition of grades can be made a subquery of the main query.

Consider the SQL query 
```sql
SELECT p.a1
FROM p, r1, r2
WHERE p.a1 = r1.a1 OR p.a1 = r2.a1
```
Under what conditions does the preceding query select values of p.a1 that are 
either in r1 or in r2 ? Examine carefully the cases where either r1 or r2 
may be empty.
questions.solution:
The query selects those values of p.a1_ that are equal to some value of _r1.a1 or 
r2.a1 if and only if both r1 and r2 are non-empty. If one or both of r1 and r2
are empty, the Cartesian product of p, r1 and r2 is empty, hence the result of the
query is empty. If p itself is empty, the result is empty.

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

Consider the relational database of Figure 3.19, where the primary keys are 
underlined. Give an expression in SQL for each of the following queries. 

a. Find the ID, name, and city of residence of each employee who works for "First Bank Corporation". 

b. Find the ID, name, and city of residence of each employee who works for "First Bank Corporation"
and earns more than USD 10000. 

c. Find the ID of each employee who does not work for "First Bank Corporation". 

d. Find the ID of each employee who earns more than every employee of "Small Bank Corporation". 

e. Assume that companies may be located in several cities. Find the name of each company that 
is located in every city in which "Small Bank Corporation" is located. 

f. Find the name of the company that has the most employees (or companies, in the case where 
there is a tie for the most). 

g. Find the name of each company whose employees earn a higher salary, on average, than the 
average salary at "First Bank Corporation".
questions.solution:
a. Find the ID, name, and city of residence of each employee who works for "First Bank Corporation".

```sql
SELECT e.ID, e.person_name, city
FROM employee AS e, works AS w
WHERE w.company_name = 'First Bank Corporation' AND w.ID = e.ID
```

b. Find the ID, name, and city of residence of each employee who works for "First Bank Corporation"
and earns more than USD 10000.

```sql 
SELECT ID, name, city
FROM employee 
WHERE ID IN (
    SELECT ID
    FROM works
    WHERE company_name = 'First Bank Corporation' AND salary > 10000
) 
```

This could be written also in the style of the answer to part a, as follows: 

```sql
SELECT e.ID, e.person_name, city
FROM employee AS e, works AS w
WHERE w.company_name = 'First Bank Corporation' AND w.ID = e.ID
    AND w.salary > 10000
```

c. Find the ID of each employee who does not work for "First Bank Corporation".

```sql
SELECT ID
FROM works
WHERE company_name <> 'First Bank Corporation' 
```

If one allows people to appear in employee without appearing also in 
works, the solution is slightly more complicated. An outer join as discussed
in Chapter 4 could be used as well. 

```sql 
SELECT ID 
FROM employee
WHERE ID NOT IN (
    SELECT ID
    FROM works
    WHERE company_name = 'First Bank Corporation'
)
```

d. Find the ID of each employee who earns more than every employee of "Small Bank Corporation".

```sql
SELECT ID
FROM works
WHERE salary > ALL (
    SELECT salary
    FROM works
    WHERE company_name = 'Small Bank Corporation'
)
```

If people may work for several companies and we wish to consider the total earnings of 
each person, the is more complex. But note that the fact that ID is the primary key for 
works implies that this cannot be the case. 

e. Assume that companies may be located in several cities. Find the name of each company that 
is located in every city in which "Small Bank Corporation" is located.

```sql 
SELECT S.company_name 
FROM company AS S 
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    (
        SELECT city
        FROM company
        WHERE company_name = 'Small Bank Corporation'
    )
    EXCEPT
    (
        SELECT city
        FROM company AS T
        WHERE T.company_name = S.company_name
    )
)
```

f. Find the name of the company that has the most employees (or companies, in the case where 
there is a tie for the most).

```sql
SELECT company_name 
FROM works
GROUP BY company_name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ID) >= ALL (
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ID)
    FROM works
    GROUP BY company_name
)
```

g. Find the name of each company whose employees earn a higher salary, on average, than the 
average salary at "First Bank Corporation".

```sql
SELECT company_name
FROM works
GROUP BY company_name 
HAVING AVG(salary) >  (
    SELECT AVG(salary)
    FROM works
    WHERE company_name = 'First Bank Corporation'
)
```

Consider the relational database of Figure 3.19. Give an expression in SQL 
for each of the following: 

a. Modify the database so that the employee whose ID is '12345' now lives in 
"Newtown". 

b. Give each manager of "First Bank Corporation" a 10 percent raise unless
the salary becomes greater than USD 100000; in such cases, give only a 3 percent
raise.
questions.solution:
a. Modify the database so that the employee whose ID is '12345' now lives in "Newtown".

```sql
UPDATE employee
SET city = 'Newtown'
WHERE ID = '12345' 
```

b. Give each manager of "First Bank Corporation" a 10 percent raise unless
the salary becomes greater than USD 100000; in such cases, give only a 3 percent
raise.

```sql
UPDATE works T
SET T.salary = T.salary * 1.03
WHERE T.ID IN (SELECT manager_id FROM manages)
    AND T.salary * 1.1 > 100000
    AND T.company_name = 'First Bank Corporation';

UPDATE works T
SET T.salary = T.salary * 1.1
WHERE T.ID IN (SELECT manager_id FROM manages)
    AND T.salary * 1.1 <= 100000
    AND T.company_name = 'First Bank Corporation';
```

The above updates would give different results if executed in the opposite 
order. We give below a safer solution using the case statement. 

```sql
UPDATE works T
SET T.salary = T.salary * ( 
    CASE
        WHEN (T.salary * 1.1 > 100000) THEN 1.03
        ELSE 1.1 
    END
)
WHERE T.ID IN (SELECT manager_id FROM manages) 
    AND T.company_name = 'First Bank Corporation'
```

questions.solution:
a. Create a new course "CS-001", titled "Weekly Seminar", with 0 credits.

```sql
INSERT INTO course (course_id, title,dept_name, credits) 
VALUES ('CS-001','Weekly Seminar','Comp. Sci.', 0);
```

b. Create a section of this course in Fall 2017, with sec_id of 1, and with the location 
of this section not yet specified.

```sql
INSERT INTO section (course_id, sec_id, semester, year) VALUES 
('CS-001', '1', 'Fall', 2017)
```

c. Enroll every student in the Comp. Sci. department in the above section.

```sql 
INSERT INTO takes (id, course_id, sec_id, semester, year) 
SELECT student.id,'CS-001', '1', 'Fall', 2017
FROM student 
WHERE student.dept_name = 'Comp. Sci.'
```

d. Delete enrollments in the above section where the student's ID is 12345.

```sql 
DELETE FROM takes 
WHERE ID = '12345' AND (course_id, sec_id, semester, year) = ('CS-001', '1', 'Fall', 2017)
```

without first deleting offerings (sections) of this course? 

To delete the course CS-001 we use the following query: 

```sql
DELETE FROM course
WHERE course_id = 'CS-001'; 
```

Below we can see the schema of the section relation. Taken from db-book.com.

```sql 
create table section
        (course_id              varchar(8),
         sec_id                 varchar(8),
         semester               varchar(6)
                check (semester in ('Fall', 'Winter', 'Spring', 'Summer')),
         year                   numeric(4,0) check (year > 1701 and year < 2100),
         building               varchar(15),
         room_number            varchar(7),
         time_slot_id           varchar(4),
         primary key (course_id, sec_id, semester, year),
         foreign key (course_id) references course (course_id)
                on delete cascade,
         foreign key (building, room_number) references classroom (building, room_number)
                on delete set null
        );
```

In the above query we see ON DELETE CASCADE. This means when any course tuple is deleted
all corresponding section tuples will also be deleted. Therefore when you delete CS-001 all
the corresponding rows in the section relation will also be deleted. 

 

f. Delete all takes tuples corresponding to any section of any course with 
the word "advanced" as a part of the title; ignore case when matching the word 
with the title. 

```sql
DELETE FROM takes
WHERE course_id IN (
    SELECT course_id
    FROM course
    WHERE LOWER(title) LIKE '%advanced%'
)
```

Consider the employee database of Figure 3.19, where the primary keys are underlined. 
Given an expression in SQL for each of the following queries. 

a. Find ID and name of each employee who lives in the same city as the location 
of the company for which the employee works. 
 
b. Find ID and name of each employee who lives in the same city and on the same 
street as does her or his manager. 
 
c. Find ID and name of each employee who earns more than the average salary of 
all employees of her or his company. 

d. Find the company that has the smallest payroll.
questions.solution:
a. Find ID and name of each employee who lives in the same city as the location 
of the company for which the employee works.

```sql
SELECT employee.id, employee.person_name
FROM employee INNER JOIN works ON employee.id = works.id
              INNER JOIN company ON works.company_name = company.company_name
WHERE employee.city = company.city
```

b. Find ID and name of each employee who lives in the same city and on the same 
street as does her or his manager.

```sql 
SELECT E.id, E.person_name
FROM employee AS E INNER JOIN manages ON E.id = manages.id
                   INNER JOIN employee AS manager_of_E ON manages.manager_id = manager_of_E.id
WHERE E.street = manager_of_E.street AND 
      E.city = manager_of_E.city;
```

c. Find ID and name of each employee who earns more than the average salary of 
all employees of her or his company.

```sql
WITH average_salary_per_company(company_name, avg_salary) AS (
    SELECT company_name, AVG(salary) 
    FROM works
    GROUP BY company_name
) 
SELECT E.id, E.person_name
FROM employee AS E INNER JOIN works ON E.id = works.id
WHERE works.salary > (
    SELECT avg_salary 
    FROM average_salary_per_company 
    WHERE company_name = works.company_name
)
```

d. Find the company that has the smallest payroll.

```sql
SELECT company_name, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll
FROM works
GROUP BY company_name
ORDER BY total_payroll ASC
LIMIT 1
```

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

Show that, in SQL, $<>$ ALL is identical to NOT IN.
questions.solution:
Let r1 and r2 be two relations having only one attribute say k.

Let the following be called "query 1".

```sql 
SELECT k
FROM r1
WHERE k <> ALL (
    SELECT k
    FROM r2
)
```

Let the following be called "query 2".

```sql 
SELECT k
FROM r1
WHERE k NOT IN (
    SELECT k
    FROM r2
)
```

As you can see query 1 and query 2 are almost the same, except we replaced "<> ALL"
in query 1 by "NOT IN" in query 2. If we can show that the two queries give the same
result i.e. the same set of tuples, we have shown that $<>$ ALL is identical to NOT IN.

 

Take any tuple from the result of query 1, say $t_1$. Since $t_1$ is in relation $r1$ and not equal 
to any tuple of relation $r2$, it is not in relation $r2$. Therefore $t_1$ is in the result of query 2. 

Take any tuple from the result of query 2, say $t_2$. Since $t_2$ is in relation $r1$ and not in 
relation $r2$, it is not equal to any tuple of relation $r2$. Therefore $t_2$ is in the result of query 1. 

 

Thus the result of the two queries is identical. 

 

Which proves in general case that $<>$ ALL is identical to NOT IN.

Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

Consider the library database of Figure 3.20. Write the following queries in SQL. 

a. Find the member number and name of each member who has borrowed at least one book 
published by "McGraw-Hill". 

b. Find the member number and name of each member who has borrowed every book published by "McGraw-Hill".

c. For each publisher, find the member number and name of each member who has borrowed more than five books
of that publisher. 
 
d. Find the average number of books borrowed per member. Take into account that if a member does not 
borrow any books, then that member does not appear in the borrowed relation at all, but that member still
counts in the average.
questions.solution:
a. Find the member number and name of each member who has borrowed at least one book 
published by "McGraw-Hill". 
 

```sql
SELECT memb_no, name
FROM member AS m
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT * 
    FROM book INNER JOIN borrowed ON book.isbn = borrowed.isbn 
    WHERE book.publisher = 'McGraw-Hill' AND 
            borrowed.memb_no = m.memb_no
)
```

b. Find the member number and name of each member who has borrowed every book published by "McGraw-Hill".

```sql
SELECT memb_no, name
FROM member AS m 
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    (
        SELECT isbn
        FROM book
        WHERE publisher = 'McGraw-Hill'
    )
    EXCEPT 
    (
        SELECT isbn
        FROM borrowed
        WHERE memb_no = m.memb_no
    )
) 
```

c. For each publisher, find the member number and name of each member who has borrowed more than five books
of that publisher.

```sql
WITH member_borrowed_book(memb_no, memb_name,isbn,title,authors,publisher,date) AS (
    SELECT member.memb_no, name, book.isbn, title, authors, publisher, date
    FROM member INNER JOIN borrowed ON member.memb_no = borrowed.memb_no
                INNER JOIN book ON borrowed.isbn = book.isbn
)
SELECT memb_no, memb_name, publisher, COUNT(isbn)
FROM member_borrowed_book
GROUP BY memb_no, memb_name, publisher
HAVING COUNT(isbn) > 5;
```

d. Find the average number of books borrowed per member. Take into account that if a member does not 
borrow any books, then that member does not appear in the borrowed relation at all, but that member still
counts in the average.

```sql 
WITH number_of_books_borrowed(memb_no, memb_name, number_of_books) AS (
    SELECT memb_no, name, (
        CASE
            WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM borrowed WHERE borrowed.memb_no = member.memb_no) THEN 0
            ELSE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM borrowed WHERE borrowed.memb_no = member.memb_no) 
        END
    )
    FROM member
)
SELECT AVG(number_of_books) AS average_number_of_books_borrowed_per_member
FROM number_of_books_borrowed
```

questions.prompt:
Select the option that best answers the exercise below.

Consider the following SQL query on the university schema: 

```sql
SELECT AVG(salary) - (SUM(salary)/COUNT(*))
FROM instructor
```

We might expect that the result of this query is zero since the average 
of a set of numbers is defined to be the sum of the numbers divided by 
the number of numbers. Indeed this is true for the example instructor
relation in Figure 2.1. However, there are other possible instances
of that relation for which the result would not be zero. Give one such
instance, and explain why the result would not be zero.
questions.solution:
Consider the following instance of the instructor relation. 

```
university=# SELECT * FROM instructor;
  id   |    name    | dept_name  |  salary   
-------+------------+------------+-----------
 12121 | Wu         | Finance    |  90000.00
 15151 | Mozart     | Music      |  40000.00
 1     | Tesla      | Elec. Eng. |   NULL       
(3 rows)
```

Then using the previous query will not give 0 as shown below:- 

```
university=# SELECT AVG(salary) - (SUM(salary)/COUNT(*))
university-# FROM instructor
university-# ;
      ?column?      

 21666.666666666667
(1 row)

university=# 
```

This is because of the NULL salary of the instructor 'Tesla'. 

 

All aggregate functions except count(*) ignore null values in their input collection. 

Thus AVG(salary) computes: 

$$
    \frac {90000 + 40000} {2} = \frac {130000} {2} = 65000.0
$$

While _SUM(salary)/COUNT(*)_ computes: 

$$
    \frac {SUM(salary)}{COUNT(*)} = \frac {90000 + 40000} {3} = \frac {130000} {3} = 43333.333333333336
$$

Write the following queries in SQL: 

a. Display a list of all instructors, showing each instructor's ID and the number of sections
taught. Make sure to show the number of sections as 0 for instructors who have not taught any
section. Your query should use an outer join, and should not use subqueries. 

b. Write the same query as in part a, but using a scalar subquery and not using outer join. 

c. Display the list of all course sections offered in Spring 2018, along with the ID and name
of each instructor teaching the section. If a section has more than one instructor, that section
should appear as many times in the result as it has instructors. If a section does not have 
any instructor, it should still appear in the result with the instructor name set to "-". 

d. Display the list of all departments, with the total number of instructors, in each department,
without using subqueries. Make sure to show departments that have no instructors, and list those 
departments with an instructor count of zero.
questions.solution:
a. Display a list of all instructors, showing each instructor's ID and the number of sections
taught. Make sure to show the number of sections as 0 for instructors who have not taught any
section. Your query should use an outer join, and should not use subqueries

```sql
SELECT ID, COUNT(sec_id) AS Number_of_sections
FROM instructor NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN teaches
GROUP BY ID
```

The above query should not be written using COUNT(*) since that would count null values also. 
It could be written using any attribute from teaches which does not occur in instructor, 
which would be correct although it may be confusing to the reader. (Attributes that occur in 
instructor would not be null even if the instructor has not taught any section.)

b. Write the same query as in part a, but using a scalar subquery and not using outerjoin.

```sql
SELECT ID, (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS Number_of_sections
    FROM teaches T
    WHERE T.id = I.id
)
FROM instructor I
```

c. Display the list of all course sections offered in Spring 2018, along with the ID and name
of each instructor teaching the section. If a section has more than one instructor, that section
should appear as many times in the result as it has instructors. If a section does not have 
any instructor, it should still appear in the result with the instructor name set to "-".

```sql
SELECT course_id,sec_id,ID,decode(name,null,'-',name) as name
FROM (section NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN teaches)
    NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN instructor
WHERE semester = 'Spring' AND year = 2018;
```

The query may also be written using the coalesce operator, by replacing decode(..)
with coalesce(name,'-'). A more complex version of the query can be written using union of
join result with another query that uses a subquery to find courses that do not match; refer to 
Exercise 4.3.

```sql
-- using coalesce
SELECT course_id,sec_id,ID,coalesce(name,'-') as name
FROM (section NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN teaches)
    NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN instructor
WHERE semester = 'Spring' AND year = 2018;
```

d. Display the list of all departments, with the total number of instructors, in each department,
without using subqueries. Make sure to show departments that have no instructors, and list those 
departments with an instructor count of zero.

```sql
SELECT dept_name, COUNT(id)
FROM department NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN instructor
GROUP BY dept_name;
```

a. In Section 4.1.1 we saw an example of an erroneous SQL query which

and course. Give an example of a dataset that would help catch this particular
